title: Hormuz closure: the maritime risk-transfer and rerouting chain beneath the oil price
map_limitation: Four blind spots specific to THIS map. (1) The root is unbuyable and publishes nothing: the strait is held by the IRGC and the transit charge was run by the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, an Iranian body the United States sanctioned, which never published a fee schedule. Every toll figure on this map is a third-party estimate, hormuz-transit-control carries zero tickers by design, and the pool the appraisal identified as the largest by rate of collection has no instrument at any price. (2) The two layers this occurrence repriced hardest are structurally unlisted, so supplier-side EDGAR full-text search cannot reach them. The liability half of marine war risk is written by mutuals with no equity at all (Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, the London P&I Club, the American Club and the rest of the International Group), the intelligence and protection layer is private (Ambrey, Constellis, Dryad Global, Risk Intelligence, Kpler, Windward, Lloyd's List Intelligence), the bunker names expanding into the Cape trade are private (Monjasa, Vitol, Bunker Partner, Peninsula, Flex Commodities, Global Fuel Supply), the manning agencies paying the war bonuses are private, and the bypass pipelines are state assets. maritime-risk-and-protection therefore carries one ticker and crew-and-warlike-area-manning carries none, and that is a finding about the chain, not a gap in the search. (3) The listed names that matter mostly file outside the SEC and reach this map through research rather than through fts: BEZ.L, HSX.L, LRE.L, ALV.DE, ZURN.SW, 8766.T, 8725.T, MUV2.DE, SREN.SW, HNR1.DE, SCR.PA, OET.OL, TRMD-A.CO, HAFN.OL, 9104.T, 9101.T, 1138.HK, FLNG.OL, MAERSK-B.CO, HLAG.DE, 2603.TW, 2609.TW, 011200.KS, 601919.SS, 2222.SR, VPK.AS, EXA.PA, SAAB-B.ST, KOG.OL, HO.PA, LDO.MI, BA.L, FCT.MI, EQNR.OL, WDS.AX, RELIANCE.NS, IOC.NS, 5020.T, 010950.KS, 0386.HK, TOP.BK, 9531.T, SHEL.L, BP.L and TTE.PA. (4) Three quantities the thesis rests on are directionally sourced and quantitatively soft. Every freight rate here is a trade-press print of an LSEG or Baltic assessment quoted secondhand, not a fetched series, so no rate on this map can be re-derived in this repo. War-risk premium is a broker-quoted percentage of hull value with a 1% to 10% spread across the cited sources, and no issuer discloses Gulf war-risk premium income separately, so the split between the primary book, the reinsurance layer and the state backstop cannot be sized from any filing. And the Joint War Committee's listed areas now cover the Red Sea and the Gulf together, while no cited source splits premium or claims between this occurrence and the pre-existing Houthi book, which makes double-counting the two the most likely quiet error on this map.

scenarios.title: Negotiated reopening and fast normalisation
scenarios.narrative: The stated condition is met, the memorandum is accepted and the strait reopens under an agreement. Traffic returns over weeks rather than quarters, the Cape detour unwinds and the effective fleet comes back all at once. The warlike-area designation is lifted with the closure, so crew consent stops being a constraint and the bonus disappears. Hull war rates fall back toward the fraction of hull value they were before the conflict, and the risk-transfer layer gives back the rate without ever having earned the loss ratio. The cost stack unwinds fastest where it built fastest, which is freight.

links_moved.why: The toll regime exists only while the closure does. Reopening under an agreement ends the per-vessel charge and with it the only pricing power on this link.

About a third of effective capacity is absorbed by the detour rather than by demand. Remove roughly 14 days a leg and the effective fleet returns in one step, which is the fastest possible unwind of a record rate.
The right to refuse is triggered by the danger designation. Lift it and the six-month bonus stops being necessary, so the cost transfer ends.
Cover repriced from 1 to 3 percent of hull value up to 7.5 to 10 percent on the closure. A reopening removes the peril that justified the range and the primary book gives most of it back.
Commission scales with the premium base, so the broker gives back the uplift, but keeps the placement volume as traffic returns, which is why this is medium and the underwriter is large.
The extra burn was the extra distance. A 56 percent longer voyage reverts and the buying moves back into the Gulf hubs it left.
Cargoes resume through the strait, but train damage still caps Ras Laffan loadings, so the carrier gives back less than the crude tanker does.
The panic bid goes, but the cumulative supply gap runs to 2030 and the authorised capacity is already being built, so the structural demand for non-Gulf molecules survives the reopening.

notes.text: THE THESIS WAS TESTED AND IT SURVIVES WITH ONE STRUCTURAL CORRECTION. The signal names four unmapped layers: tanker rerouting and ton-mile, marine war-risk underwriting and the reinsurance behind it, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority transit toll, and the private maritime-security layer. All four are on this map and all four cite separately. The correction is that a fifth layer sits above three of them and nobody in the coverage names it: crew consent. The Lloyd's Market Association, surveying its own underwriters, states in terms that the reason ships are not moving is not a lack of insurance but the risk to crew and vessel safety as assessed by masters and owners, with 88% of respondents still willing to write hull war risk. The world's largest supertanker owner is separately reported offering six months' extra pay for a one-month round trip, and crews are still refusing. So the binding constraint on this chain is not underwriting capacity, which is what the insurance framing implies; it is willingness to sail. That is why crew-and-warlike-area-manning is a CHOKE_POINT with zero tickers and why marine-war-risk-underwriting is HIGH rather than CHOKE_POINT.

FLOWS ARE KEPT SEPARATE FROM REVENUES, per the appraisal's refusal to round the money leg up on a trade-flow figure. Three numbers on this map are flows and are never treated as pools: around 20 million barrels a day of transit, roughly a fifth of world LNG, and 470,000 TEUs of trapped container capacity. Three are collected revenues or committed capacity and are treated as such: the $20 billion DFC facility, the $200 million per line Lloyd's consortium, and the freight and premium prints (a record $647,000 a day Gulf-to-Asia, war risk at 7.5 to 10 percent of hull value, $77.96 a tonne of crude, a $3,000/FEU box surcharge). The toll sits in a third category and is named as such on hormuz-transit-control: a real collection with no instrument.

SHARED LINK DECLARED. war-risk-reinsurance-capacity is the one link this chain shares with offshore-counter-drone (rank 9, built separately): the Lloyd's syndicate and reinsurance capital layer is common to both. The books are NOT the same and the maps must not merge them. This chain's underwriting link, marine-war-risk-underwriting, is war risk on MOVING HULLS: war hull, war P&I and war cargo on vessels under way, listed by the Joint War Committee, cancellable at seven days' notice and repriced per voyage. offshore-counter-drone covers FIXED offshore installations, which is an energy and property book with a different loss model and a different renewal cycle. The only genuine overlap is the retrocession and Lloyd's capacity behind both, plus one issuer: CB appears on this chain twice already and is likely to appear on that one too, so a position in Chubb is one bet on the Gulf, not three.

ARCHETYPES. Applied: ARCH-003 (uninvestable order-book owner, inverted) on hormuz-transit-control, the third chain in a row where the root of the map is a sanctioned or state party that publishes nothing; ARCH-006 (geopolitical counter-response as a first-class link) twice, on naval-escort-and-mine-clearance and on non-gulf-energy-substitution, which takes ARCH-006 to its second chain and is the recurrence its Watch note was asking for; ARCH-004 (critical material, criticality equals substitutability times logistics) on bunker-and-voyage-services in its logistics-dominant form, the same mechanism that made cement regional on tibet-mega-dam; ARCH-002 (volume without capture) checked and NOT built as a link, because the only EPC scope here is a roughly $3 billion pipeline expansion that cannot carry a link of its own, so it is recorded inside hormuz-bypass-pipelines instead. Checked and did not fire: ARCH-001 (precision manufacturing capacity as the gating step), because the capacity that gates this chain is voyage time on an existing fleet and not a production line, and no cited source ties this occurrence to shipyard ordering; ARCH-005 (power and grid equipment behind someone else's story), no grid layer on this map; ARCH-007 (semis as a leaf), the nearest analogue is the satellite and analytics layer, which is folded into maritime-risk-and-protection rather than given a compute link it does not deserve.

STAGES CHECKED AND NOT BUILT, each because nothing citable tied it to this occurrence. (1) Shipyard and newbuild capacity: the fleet response to a third of capacity being absorbed by voyage length would normally be ordering, and no fetched source connects Hormuz to tanker ordering, so it is not a stage on this map. (2) Kidnap-and-ransom and hijack response: the Somali hijackings with reported multi-million dollar ransom demands imply a K&R and negotiation market, and the one article that would have established it returned HTTP 403, so it stays out rather than being cited from a search snippet. (3) Floating storage and ship-to-ship transfer: plausible from the reported hundreds of vessels anchored off Gulf coasts, but no fetched source establishes it as a commercial stage with its own economics. (4) Transshipment hub substitution away from Jebel Ali: named in liner coverage but never quantified in anything that opened. (5) Marine war-risk claims adjusting and salvage: no cited source establishes claims activity at all, which is itself the finding, because premium with no visible claims is the thing the heat stage most needs to test. Four URLs were fetched and refused: the World Economic Forum's insurers-of-last-resort piece (403), S&P Global's Marsh premium report (403), CNBC's Somali piracy and maritime-drone articles (403), and Splash247 on armed guard pricing (403). The Howden Re reinsurance report returned an unreadable PDF and was not cited. None of those five refused pages contributed a link or an edge.
